UNIT 4: MAP SKILLS
Unifying Strand: Applying Geographical Thinking and Skills.

LEARNING OUTCOMES (U2, U7, U9)
- Read and sketch maps of various scales.
- Analyse and synthesise geographical data using Tailte Eireann (TE) maps.
- Communicate geographical understanding using TE maps.

WHAT IS A MAP?
- A map is a plan of an area of the Earth's surface that is drawn to scale.
- Scale gives a measurable relationship between a distance on the map and the actual distance on the ground.
- Without scale, a map is nothing more than an elaborate drawing.
- Maps show the spatial relationship between things by distance, direction and size.

THE NATIONAL GRID
- On TE maps, the island of Ireland is divided into 25 squares called subzones.
- Subzones are lettered A to Z, leaving out the letter I.
- These 25 squares make up the National Grid.

DISCOVERY SERIES MAPS
- The most commonly used TE maps.
- Scale 1:50,000 - 2 cm on paper represents 1 km on the ground. So each grid square (2 cm x 2 cm) is 1 km2.
- 93 maps in the series cover the island of Ireland: 75 produced by TE and 18 by the Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland.

UNDERSTANDING SCALE
- Every map has a scale showing the relationship between map distance and ground distance. It is usually at the base of the map's legend.
- Three ways to show scale:
- 1. Representative fraction (RF): a ratio, e.g. 1:50,000 - 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm on the ground.
- 2. Linear scale: a line divided into kilometres.
- 3. Statement of scale: written in words, e.g. 2 cm to 1 km.
- Small-scale maps show large areas with little detail, e.g. a map of the world or of Europe - maybe only capital cities, borders and big physical features like mountain ranges. Example: 1:50,000 map of Ballina, Co. Mayo.
- Large-scale maps show smaller areas in greater detail. Street maps show outlines of buildings, whereas 1:50,000 maps do not. Examples: street map of Kilkenny Castle and nearby streets; a 1:10,000 TE map of Blessington, where 10 cm = 1 km.

WORKING WITH SYMBOLS
- Some objects are too small or awkward to draw to scale, so they are shown as symbols, e.g. roads, railway lines, streams. Symbols are not drawn to scale.
- Most symbols are on the legend sheet, usually on the back of the map (Figure 4.8: the TE Discovery Series legend).
- Features NOT labelled on the legend:
- 1. Individual houses in rural areas: shown as a small black square dot.
- 2. Rural settlement patterns: linear, nucleated (clustered) and dispersed. Examples: linear settlement at Aillemore, Co. Mayo; clustered settlement at Athenry, Co. Galway.
- 3. Antiquities: usually labelled in red. Ringforts are shown by a red circle. Examples: castle, megalithic tomb.
- 4. Drainage patterns of rivers and streams: dendritic, radial, trellised and deranged.

FINDING DIRECTION
- All TE maps have a North arrow, which always points up, so the top of the map is North.
- Knowing North lets you work out the other 15 compass points (16 points in total).
- The four main points - North, South, East and West - are called cardinal points.
- How to find direction: mark the starting point A (or X); draw a straight pencil line with a ruler to the point B; using the North arrow, draw a compass at A (cardinal points first, then the others); read which compass point matches your line to B.

GRID REFERENCES
FOUR-FIGURE GRID REFERENCES
- Used to locate an entire square.
- 1. Give the subzone letter. 2. Give the two-digit easting (vertical line) to the LEFT of the square. 3. Give the two-digit northing (horizontal line) at the BOTTOM of the square.
- Worked example: Lough Agraffard = M 06 42 (letter M, easting 06, northing 42).
- Memory aid: LEN (Letter, Easting, Northing).
- At Senior Cycle, use four-figure references only for large areas: a lake, forestry, a large island, a town.
- The subzone letter can be anywhere on the map.
SIX-FIGURE GRID REFERENCES
- Used to locate a specific point within a square.
- 1. Divide the square into ten equal parts along the easting and northing (each square is 2 cm x 2 cm).
- 2. Subzone letter. 3. Two-digit easting to the left (leave space for a third figure). 4. Two-digit northing at the bottom (leave space for a sixth figure).
- 5. Count how many tenths ACROSS the bottom the object is - the third figure.
- 6. Count how many tenths UP the side the object is - the sixth figure.
- Worked example: spot height 158 at Derryerglinna, Galway: letter M, easting 05, across the bottom 3, northing 43, along the side 8 = M 053 438.
- Memory aid: LEN ABAS (Letter, Easting, Northing, Across the Bottom, Along the Side). The summary calls it LENABAS.
- At Senior Cycle most features are located with six-figure references, e.g. a spot height on a peak, a parking area or a train station.

MEASURING DISTANCE
STRAIGHT-LINE DISTANCE ('AS THE CROW FLIES')
- 1. Mark two points A and B. 2. Draw a straight line between them. 3. Place the straight edge of a piece of paper along the line. 4. Mark the paper at A and at B.
- 5. Place the paper against the map's linear scale or a ruler. On the linear scale, put point B at the last full kilometre. With a ruler, convert cm to km (2 cm = 1 km).
CURVED-LINE DISTANCE (e.g. along a road)
- 1. Put the straight edge of paper at the start; mark both paper and map.
- 2. Mark where the road makes its first turn; turn the paper to line up with the road and mark again.
- 3. Keep marking and turning until the end point.
- 4. Place the paper against the scale bar starting at 0 (not the beginning of the line) and read the length in km; or use a ruler and convert (2 cm = 1 km).
- 5. You can use a piece of string - keep your thumb tight on it at each bend.
- 6. You can also use an opisometer (a small measuring wheel tool).

CALCULATING AREA
- Regular-shaped area: length x width. Count full grid squares across the base and along the side and multiply. Each square = 1 km2, so the answer is in km2.
- Irregular-shaped area (lake, harbour, forest, town):
- 1. Tick (red) all squares fully filled by the feature.
- 2. Tick (green) all squares at least half-filled; ignore those less than half-filled.
- 3. If unsure, divide the square in half with a ruler and pencil line.
- 4. Count red ticks as whole squares and green ticks as halves; add them. The total is the approximate area in km2.
- Worked example (Figure 4.16): 4 full squares + 8 half-filled squares (8 halves = 4) = 8 km2.
- Practice: Tramore Bay area under water.

RELIEF AND HEIGHT
- Height in Ireland is measured from Mean Sea Level (MSL) at Malin Head, Co. Donegal, known as Ordnance Datum (OD).
- Mean Sea Level: the average height of the sea surface over a long period, taking tides into account. Malin Head readings were taken between 1960 and 1969. Since 1970 all TE maps use Malin Head as Ordnance Datum. Before that, it was at Poolbeg, Dublin.
- Height is shown in metres above sea level in four ways:
- 1. Colour: changes every 100 m; the higher the land, the darker the shade.
- 2. Contour lines: join places of equal height above sea level; drawn at 10 m intervals. Index contours (stronger lines, often at 50 m, 100 m, 200 m and 250 m) always have heights marked.
- 3. Triangulation pillars (stations): concrete pillars on summits of hills and mountains marking exact height; shown by a black triangle with the height.
- 4. Spot heights: height at various points; shown as a black dot with a number (metres).

SLOPE AND AVERAGE GRADIENT
- Slope is also called gradient. It is shown by the pattern of contour lines.
- Widely spaced contours = gentle slope. Close contours = steep slope.
- Four slope types (Figure 4.22, Ben Gorm):
- Even (regular) slope: contours evenly spaced.
- Concave slope: gentle at the base (contours wide apart) and much steeper near the top (contours close together).
- Convex slope: steeper at the base (contours close together) and gentle near the top (contours wider apart).
- Stepped (composite) slope: steep and gentle sections separated by gently sloping or flat sections.
- Average gradient: the ratio between the distance travelled and the height change between two points.
- Vertical Interval (VI): the difference in height between the two points.
- Horizontal Equivalent (HE): the distance in metres between the two points.
- Formula: Average Gradient = VI / HE, given as a ratio, e.g. 1:10.
- Worked example: triangulation pillar at Corrymailley L 769 719 (A) and spot height near Corryaughany L 786 721 (B). VI = 312 m - 286 m = 26 m. HE = 850 m. 26/850: divide both by 26 gives 1 : 32.7. So there is a 1 m change in height for every 32.7 m travelled.
- Geofacts: anything over 26.5 degrees is difficult to walk or climb; a 1.5 degree slope is considered very steep for a railway.

DRAWING A SKETCH MAP OF A TE MAP
- Pencil only; never trace; no grid squares; colouring not needed.
- 1. Title using the main town's name, e.g. 'Sketch map of Dingle area'.
- 2. Frame exactly half the length and half the width of the map extract (half scale - this makes the map a quarter of the size of the original). Same shape and orientation (landscape or portrait). Sometimes the frame is provided.
- 3. Lightly draw diagonal, vertical and horizontal guidelines on both the map and the sketch.
- 4. Draw the North arrow inside the frame.
- 5. Draw the coastline (if there is one) using the segments.
- 6. Draw only the features asked; label them on the map and in a key/legend. Reasonable accuracy is expected.
- 7. Roads: a thick pencil line on a TE sketch (two parallel lines are needed only for roads on an aerial photo sketch).
- 8. Built-up urban areas must have an outline, not a dot or an 'X'.
- 9. Woodland must have a boundary line around it.
- 10. Erase guidelines when finished.
- Example (Figure 4.24): sketch map of Dingle showing the Garfinny River, land over 600 m, built-up area, N59 road in the key, sea, Tra Chathail beach and cliffs.

CROSS-SECTIONS
- A cross-section is a side view of an area of landscape. It shows the relief and whether there is intervisibility between two points.
- Intervisibility: one point can be seen from another with no obstructions in the way.
- How to draw one:
- 1. Choose and locate two points (A and B).
- 2. Connect their grid references with a straight-edged strip of paper.
- 3. Mark the paper at both end points and note the heights there.
- 4. Mark the paper at each contour line in between and note each height.
- 5. Mark important features (river, road).
- 6. On graph paper draw a graph with the Y-axis as metres above sea level.
- 7. Give it a title, e.g. 'Dingle cross-section'.
- 8. Place the paper on the X-axis and mark where each contour falls.
- 9. Plot each point at its height.
- 10. Join the points to show the land.
- 11. Mark the features (river, roads) on the graph at the right height.
- Worked example (Figure 4.29-4.30): Dingle, from Q 425 029 (spot height 34 m, point A) to Q 468 028 (spot height 217 m, point B), about 5 km long, crossing rivers, The Way (Dingle Way), the R549 and the R560.

SEC EXAM SKILLS (HL SAMPLE PAPER 1, QUESTION 1)
- (i) Named antiquity: megalithic tomb, at G 704 742.
- (ii) Straight-line distance between the lighthouse on Rotten Island and the triangulation pillar on Crownarad: 5.8 km.
- Elevation profile along northing 79 from G 610 790 to G 660 790 (5 km): river at A = Ballaghdoo River; woodland at B = coniferous; slope between C and D = even slope; feature at E = lake.

SUMMARY OF MAP SKILLS
- Understand scale (2 cm = 1 km).
- Direction (cardinal and compass points).
- Straight-line and curved-line distances.
- Area (regular and irregular).
- Four- and six-figure grid references, and identifying features from a grid reference (LENABAS).
- Sketch maps of TE maps, street maps or historical maps.
- Record height and identify slope and average gradient.
- Draw a cross-section and determine intervisibility.
- Identify physical landforms (mountain, coastal, glacial, fluvial).
- Identify drainage patterns.
- Recognise settlement patterns and human influence.
- Identify communication links such as roads and railways.
- Recognise historical settlement (antiquities) from different eras, e.g. ringforts (Iron Age) and castles (Norman).
- Interpret maps using knowledge from the Senior Cycle course.
- Practice map extracts in the chapter: Dingle (Co. Kerry), Athenry and Oughterard (Co. Galway), Bantry (Co. Cork), Tramore, Galway.

rows.prompt: A map is a plan of part of the Earth's surface that is:
rows.explanation: A map is a plan of an area drawn to scale; without scale it is only a drawing.

rows.prompt: On a 1:50,000 Discovery Series map, 2 cm on the map represents:
rows.explanation: Discovery Series: 2 cm = 1 km.

rows.prompt: Scale written as a ratio, such as 1:50,000, is called a:
rows.explanation: The representative fraction shows scale as a ratio.

rows.prompt: '2 cm to 1 km' is an example of a:
rows.explanation: A statement of scale states the scale in words.

rows.prompt: Which type of map shows a large area with little detail?
rows.explanation: Small-scale maps (e.g. of Europe) show large areas with little detail.

rows.prompt: On a 1:10,000 map of Blessington, how many cm represent 1 km?
rows.explanation: The chapter states 1:10,000 means 10 cm = 1 km.

rows.prompt: How many subzones make up Ireland's National Grid?
rows.explanation: Ireland is divided into 25 lettered subzones.

rows.prompt: Which letter is NOT used to name a subzone?
rows.explanation: Subzones are lettered A-Z except I.

rows.prompt: How many Discovery Series maps cover the island of Ireland?
rows.explanation: 93 maps: 75 by TE and 18 by the Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland.

rows.prompt: On a TE map, a ringfort is shown by:
options: A black dot with a number
rows.explanation: Antiquities are in red; ringforts are red circles.

rows.prompt: How are individual rural houses shown on a TE map?
rows.explanation: Rural houses appear as small black square dots and are not on the legend.

rows.prompt: Which is a drainage pattern named in the chapter?
rows.explanation: Drainage patterns: dendritic, radial, trellised and deranged.

rows.prompt: North, South, East and West are called:
rows.explanation: The four main compass points are the cardinal points.

rows.prompt: Once you know North, how many other compass points can you work out?
rows.explanation: Knowing North lets you determine the other 15 compass points.

rows.prompt: In a four-figure grid reference, the easting is the line:
options: To the right of the square
At the top of the square
Through the centre of the square
To the left of the square
rows.explanation: Give the easting to the left and the northing at the bottom.

rows.prompt: A four-figure grid reference should be used at Senior Cycle for:
options: A large area such as a lake or town
rows.explanation: Four-figure references locate whole squares - large areas only.

rows.prompt: Letter M, easting 05, across 3, northing 43, up 8. What is the six-figure grid reference?
rows.explanation: Letter, Easting, Across the bottom, Northing, Along the side: M 053 438.

rows.prompt: The memory aid for six-figure grid references is:
rows.explanation: Letter, Easting, Northing, Across the Bottom, Along the Side.

rows.prompt: What should you use to measure the distance along a winding road?
options: Curved-line method with paper, string or an opisometer
rows.explanation: Curved-line distance uses marked paper, string or an opisometer.

rows.prompt: When placing marked paper against the scale bar, you start at:
options: The start of the bar line
rows.explanation: Place it at 0, not the beginning of the line.

rows.prompt: A feature fills 4 squares fully and 8 squares at least half. Its approximate area is:
rows.explanation: 4 full + 8 halves (= 4) = 8 km2.

rows.prompt: A rectangular area is 3 squares long and 2 squares wide on a 1:50,000 map. Its area is:
rows.explanation: Length x width = 3 x 2 = 6 km2; each square is 1 km2.

rows.prompt: Height on Irish maps is measured from Mean Sea Level at:
rows.explanation: Since 1970 Malin Head has been Ordnance Datum; before that it was Poolbeg.

rows.prompt: Contour lines on TE maps are drawn at intervals of:
rows.explanation: Contours are drawn at 10 m intervals; colour changes every 100 m.

rows.prompt: A black triangle with a number on a TE map shows a:
rows.explanation: Triangulation pillars are shown by a black triangle and height.

rows.prompt: Contour lines that are close together show:
rows.explanation: Close contours = steep; wide contours = gentle.

rows.prompt: Contours wide apart at the base and close together near the top show a:
rows.explanation: Concave slopes are gentle at the base and steep near the top.

rows.prompt: In average gradient, the difference in height between two points is the:
rows.explanation: VI = difference in height; HE = distance in metres.

rows.prompt: VI = 26 m and HE = 850 m. The average gradient is about:
rows.explanation: 26/850, dividing both by 26, gives 1:32.7.

rows.prompt: On a sketch map of a TE map, a built-up urban area should be shown as:
rows.explanation: Built-up areas must have an outline, not a dot or X.

rows.prompt: When one point on a map can be seen from another with no obstructions, this is called:
rows.explanation: A cross-section shows relief and whether there is intervisibility.

rows.prompt: On a cross-section graph, the Y-axis shows:
rows.explanation: The Y-axis is metres above sea level; distance runs along the X-axis.

rows.prompt: Name and describe the three ways scale is shown on a map.
rows.model_answer: Representative fraction: a ratio such as 1:50,000, where 1 cm represents 50,000 cm. Linear scale: a line divided into kilometres. Statement of scale: written in words, e.g. 2 cm to 1 km.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a small-scale and a large-scale map, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: A small-scale map shows a large area with little detail, such as a map of the world or Europe, showing only capital cities, borders and mountain ranges. A large-scale map shows a small area in great detail, such as a street map of Kilkenny that shows building outlines.

rows.prompt: Explain step by step how to give a six-figure grid reference.
rows.model_answer: Give the subzone letter. Give the easting line to the left of the square, then count tenths across the bottom for the third figure. Give the northing line at the bottom of the square, then count tenths up the side for the sixth figure (LEN ABAS), e.g. M 053 438.

rows.prompt: Explain how to calculate the area of an irregular feature such as a lake.
rows.model_answer: Tick all squares fully filled by the lake in one colour. Tick all squares at least half-filled in another colour and ignore those less than half-filled. Count full squares as 1 km2 and half-filled squares as halves, then add them to get the approximate area in km2.

rows.prompt: Name the four ways height is shown on TE maps.
rows.model_answer: Colour, which changes every 100 m and gets darker with height. Contour lines joining places of equal height at 10 m intervals. Triangulation pillars, shown by a black triangle and height. Spot heights, shown by a black dot with a number.

rows.prompt: Describe how contour lines show concave, convex and stepped slopes.
rows.model_answer: Concave: contours wide apart at the base and close together near the top. Convex: contours close together at the base and wider apart near the top. Stepped: steep sections with close contours separated by flat or gentle sections with wider contours.

rows.prompt: Name four types of feature that are NOT shown on the TE map legend.
rows.model_answer: Individual rural houses (small black square dots); rural settlement patterns (linear, nucleated or dispersed); antiquities, shown in red, such as ringforts as red circles; and drainage patterns such as dendritic, radial, trellised and deranged.

rows.prompt: What does a cross-section show, and what is intervisibility?
rows.model_answer: A cross-section is a side view of an area of landscape on a map. It shows the relief of the land between two points and whether there is intervisibility. Intervisibility means one point can be seen from the other with no obstructions in the way.

rows.prompt: Calculate the average gradient between a triangulation pillar at 312 m and a spot height at 286 m that are 850 m apart. Show all your workings. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Average gradient = Vertical Interval / Horizontal Equivalent. VI = 312 m - 286 m = 26 m. HE = 850 m. AG = 26 / 850. Divide both by 26: 26 / 26 = 1 and 850 / 26 = 32.7. Average gradient = 1:32.7. This means the height changes 1 m for every 32.7 m travelled.
rows.marking_scheme: Formula stated 2m. VI correct 2m. HE correct (in metres) 2m. Correct ratio 1:32.7 4m (allow 2m for correct method with arithmetic error). Max 10 marks.

rows.prompt: Draw a sketch map of a TE map extract, half the length and half the width. On it show and label: the coastline, a built-up area, a national primary road and an area of coniferous woodland. Describe in words how you would draw it. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: I would draw in pencil, never trace, and leave out grid squares. I would draw a frame exactly half the length and half the width of the extract, in the same orientation, with the title 'Sketch map of Dingle area'. I would lightly draw diagonal, vertical and horizontal guidelines on the map and the sketch, and draw a North arrow inside the frame. Using the segments I would draw the coastline first. I would outline the built-up area (not a dot or X), draw the national primary road as a thick pencil line, and draw a boundary line around the woodland. I would label each feature on the map and in a key, then erase the guidelines.
rows.marking_scheme: Frame at half scale with correct orientation 4m (graded). 4 features x 4m: shown in correct position and shape 2m + labelled on map or in key 2m. Built-up area must be outlined; woodland must have a boundary. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: (i) Explain the difference between a four-figure and a six-figure grid reference. (ii) Explain how height is measured and shown on Tailte Eireann maps. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) A four-figure grid reference (Letter, Easting, Northing) locates a whole square, e.g. a lake at M 06 42. A six-figure reference adds tenths across the bottom and along the side to locate an exact point, e.g. a spot height at M 053 438. (ii) Height is measured from Mean Sea Level at Malin Head (Ordnance Datum). It is shown by colour, contour lines at 10 m intervals, triangulation pillars and spot heights.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 4m: two clear points x 2m. (ii) 6m: Malin Head/Ordnance Datum 2m + two methods of showing height x 2m. Max 10 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain, step by step, how to draw a cross-section between two points on a Tailte Eireann map, and explain how it can show intervisibility. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: First choose the two points, A and B, and join their grid references with the straight edge of a strip of paper. Mark the paper at both end points and note the height of the land there. Then mark the paper at every contour line between them and note each height. Also mark important features, such as a river or a road. On graph paper, draw a graph with metres above sea level on the Y-axis and distance along the X-axis, and give it a title such as 'Dingle cross-section'. Place the strip on the X-axis and mark where each contour falls. Plot each point at its height and join the points to show the shape of the land. Finally, mark the features at the correct height. If there is no higher ground between the two points, they are intervisible, which means one point can be seen from the other.
rows.marking_scheme: Explanation: 10 SRPs x 2 marks. Credit each correct step (paper strip, end heights, contour marks, features, graph paper/axes, title, plotting, joining, labelling features) and a clear explanation of intervisibility. Max 20 marks.
